title: App-wide state & session
scopeHtml: App-scoped state holders (session, auth, user, connectivity, theme), where global state lives, logout cleanup, account switching, per-user DI scope, cross-feature communication, locale/config state and process-death restoration. Token refresh internals belong to A7; Flow mechanics to A1.

questions.promptHtml: What is "app-wide state" in an Android app, and where should it live?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can separate screen state from state that outlives screens, and name the right owner for each.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: App-wide state is anything more than one screen needs and that must outlive any single screen: the logged-in user/session, auth tokens, feature flags, connectivity, theme and locale. I put it behind a repository or manager class scoped to the Application (a @Singleton in Hilt), expose it as an immutable StateFlow, and back it with disk if it must survive process death. ViewModels observe it, they never own it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three lifetimes exist on Android. The official guidance (data layer and saving-states pages on developer.android.com) frames them as: screen lifetime (ViewModel), process lifetime (application-scoped objects) and install lifetime (disk). App-wide state belongs to the last two.

 Disk (Room / DataStore)      survives process death, source of truth
        ^   |
        |   v
 App-scoped holder (@Singleton) in-memory cache + StateFlow, dies with process
        |
        v
 ViewModel (screen scope)      collects, maps to UiState, dies with screen
        |
        v
 UI

The data-layer guide calls these "app-oriented operations": relevant while the app is open, canceled when the process dies, and following the Application lifecycle. It also says a class whose job is crucial to the whole app can be scoped to Application, while flow-specific state (login, registration) should be scoped to the flow owner, for example a nav graph.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Singleton
class SessionRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val store: SessionStore, // DataStore-backed
    @ApplicationScope private val scope: CoroutineScope,
) {
    val session: StateFlow<Session> = store.sessionFlow
        .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, Session.Unknown)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting it in a companion object or top-level var instead of an injectable class.
  • Exposing MutableStateFlow publicly so any feature can mutate it.
  • Treating in-memory state as durable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not keep it in the Application class itself? → It becomes a service locator and is untestable; inject a class instead.
  2. Where does theme live? → Disk (DataStore) as truth, an app-scoped flow for the live value.
  3. What about state used by only two screens? → Scope it to their nav graph, not the app.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "a singleton repository". Senior names the lifetime of each piece, the source of truth, who may write, and what happens at process death and logout.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that put "current user" in a static field discover it is null after process death on the first resume from background.

questions.promptHtml: What are the dangers of global singletons and static fields for app state on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know Android's process model from those who treat it like a server.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Statics and singletons die when the OS kills the process, but the user's task is restored as if nothing happened, so you get null or default state mid-flow. They are also shared mutable state: hidden coupling, race conditions across threads, stale data after logout, and tests that leak into each other.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Process death: Android may kill a background process any time. The activity stack is restored from saved state, a new process starts, Application.onCreate runs and every object re-initializes to its initial value. Anything you set during login in memory is gone.
  2. Stale data: a singleton cache outlives the user who populated it. After logout it still holds that user's data.
  3. Concurrency: plain var written from IO and read from main has no happens-before guarantee unless @Volatile/atomics/StateFlow.
  4. Testing: object state persists across tests in the same JVM, causing order-dependent failures.
  5. Leaks: a singleton holding an Activity, View or Context leaks it for the life of the process.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken
object CurrentUser { var user: User? = null } // null after process death, visible to all threads

// Better
@Singleton
class UserRepository @Inject constructor(private val dao: UserDao) {
    val user: Flow<User?> = dao.observeCurrent() // disk is the truth
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Singleton is fine, Hilt makes it testable": Hilt fixes construction, not lifetime.
  • Caching a Context in a singleton (use applicationContext).
  • Assuming onTerminate is ever called on a device (it is not).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a Hilt @Singleton safer than object? → Easier to fake and reset in tests, but same process lifetime and same death.
  2. How do you test process death? → "Don't keep activities" is only activity destruction; to kill the process use adb shell am kill <pkg> while the app is in background (not force-stop, which clears saved state).
  3. When is a singleton right? → Truly process-wide, rebuildable state: caches, repositories, clients.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists "memory leaks and threading". Senior adds "restored task meets reset process" and "state outliving its owner (user)".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A classic NPE cluster: crash only on resume after long background, never on a fresh launch, because a login-time static was never rebuilt.

questions.promptHtml: What survives a configuration change, what survives process death, and what does that mean for app-wide state?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic lifecycle literacy applied to architecture.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A configuration change recreates the Activity but keeps the process, so ViewModels, singletons and static fields survive. Process death kills everything in memory, including ViewModels and singletons. Only the saved-state Bundle (small, transient UI state) and persistent storage survive. So app-wide state needs a disk source of truth, and screens need to restore from IDs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the official saving-states guide:

ViewModel Saved state (SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable) Persistent storage
Config change yes yes yes
Process death no yes yes
User finishes/swipes away no no yes
Size/type memory-bound small, serializable disk-bound

Notable details from the guide: saved state is written when the Activity is stopped; it should hold small things like an ID or a query, not large objects; serializing big data on the main thread causes jank. App-wide singletons follow the ViewModel column for process death: gone.

Implication: after process death the restored back stack shows a screen that expects a logged-in user. The bootstrapping path (read session from disk, build graph) must run before that screen reads app-wide state, or the screen must tolerate an Unknown state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class OrderViewModel(handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: OrderRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val orderId: String = checkNotNull(handle["orderId"]) // survives death
    val order = repo.observe(orderId) // data reloaded from disk/net
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using onSaveInstanceState to carry a whole user object.
  • Saying "ViewModel survives process death".
  • Testing only rotation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a @Singleton survive rotation? → Yes, process is the same.
  2. Bundle size limit? → The Binder transaction buffer is about 1 MB shared per process; large saved state risks TransactionTooLargeException (verify exact behavior per API level).
  3. What if the user swipes the app away? → Saved state is dropped too; only disk remains.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can fill the table. Senior designs the restore path: ID in saved state, data from disk, session re-hydrated at startup.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash dashboards that spike on "resume after 30+ minutes" almost always trace to this gap.

questions.promptHtml: How would you expose app-wide state (say current user and theme) to many ViewModels? StateFlow, SharedFlow, or something else, and who owns the scope?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks Flow-based state design and scope ownership, not just "use StateFlow".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A read-only StateFlow per concern, owned by an app-scoped repository, produced with stateIn in an application-scoped CoroutineScope with a SupervisorJob. Writers go through methods on the repository, not by mutating the flow. ViewModels combine it into their UiState. Not SharedFlow, because state needs a current value and conflation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• StateFlow always has a value, replays the latest to new collectors, conflates, and uses equality so identical writes do nothing: exactly right for state.
  • The producing scope must outlive every collector, so inject an @ApplicationScope scope rather than using a ViewModel scope (when that ViewModel dies the flow stops).
  • SharingStarted.Eagerly for cheap, always-needed state (session) so the first value is hot before any screen asks; WhileSubscribed(5_000) for expensive upstreams (a DB observer for a large dataset).
  • Initial value must be honest: use a sealed Unknown/Loading rather than a fake default, otherwise you flash wrong UI (see session modeling).
  • Immutability: expose StateFlow<T> not MutableStateFlow<T>; data classes immutable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Singleton
class ThemeRepository @Inject constructor(
    store: ThemeStore,
    @ApplicationScope scope: CoroutineScope,
) {
    val theme: StateFlow<ThemeMode?> = store.themeFlow
        .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null) // null = not loaded yet
    suspend fun set(mode: ThemeMode) = store.write(mode)
}

class HomeViewModel @Inject constructor(user: UserRepository, theme: ThemeRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val ui = combine(user.user, theme.theme) { u, t -> HomeUi(u, t) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), HomeUi.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• val state = MutableStateFlow(...) public.
  • Scope created with CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) and no SupervisorJob: one failure kills it for the process.
  • Default value that looks real (ThemeMode.Light) shown before the real one loads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not LiveData? → Fine historically; StateFlow works off Android and composes with operators.
  2. Why not SharedFlow? → No current value; late subscribers miss the state.
  3. Two sources must update atomically? → Emit one combined immutable object, not two flows that can be observed inconsistent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says StateFlow. Senior justifies the producing scope, start policy and honest initial value.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A singleton flow created in a viewModelScope stopped updating after that screen closed, so other screens showed a frozen user name.

questions.promptHtml: How do you model session/auth state so the app does not flash the login screen for a logged-in user on cold start?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic impossible-state and startup-race problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Model it as three states, not a boolean: Unknown (still reading disk), LoggedOut, LoggedIn(user). Routing is gated: while Unknown the app shows the splash and does not navigate. The decision is made once the first real value arrives.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A Boolean isLoggedIn = false default conflates "not loaded" with "logged out", so the first frame navigates to login, then jumps to home when DataStore returns, or worse leaves back-stack garbage. A sealed type removes the impossible interpretation.

 cold start -> Unknown --(disk read ok, token present)--> LoggedIn
                      \--(no token)--------------------> LoggedOut
 LoggedIn --(logout / refresh token revoked)--> LoggedOut

Keep the splash up with installSplashScreen().setKeepOnScreenCondition { session.value is Session.Unknown } (androidx.core splashscreen). Make routing a pure function of session state in one place (a root composable or a single-activity host), not scattered if (!loggedIn) startActivity(Login) in each screen. "Token present" is not "token valid": treat validity as server truth discovered on the first request, and handle revocation by transitioning to LoggedOut from the auth layer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Session {
    data object Unknown : Session
    data object LoggedOut : Session
    data class LoggedIn(val userId: String) : Session
}

@Composable
fun Root(session: Session) = when (session) {
    Session.Unknown -> Unit // splash still showing
    Session.LoggedOut -> AuthGraph()
    is Session.LoggedIn -> MainGraph(session.userId)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blocking the main thread on a DataStore read to avoid the Unknown state (ANR risk, though a short bounded read at splash is a known trade-off).
  • Each screen redirecting on its own, producing double navigation.
  • Not clearing the back stack on transition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the token is expired? → Stay LoggedIn until a request proves it; refresh transparently; go LoggedOut only when refresh fails definitively.
  2. Offline cold start? → Still LoggedIn; do not require network to render home.
  3. Deep link while Unknown? → Hold the pending intent, route after state resolves.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE uses a boolean plus a splash delay. Senior removes the impossible state and centralizes routing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 300 ms login-screen flash for returning users showed up as a funnel drop in analytics ("login screen viewed" by logged-in users).

questions.promptHtml: How would you provide connectivity state app-wide, and why is "is connected" a trap?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real-world API knowledge and awareness of lying signals.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Wrap ConnectivityManager.registerDefaultNetworkCallback in a callbackFlow, expose a StateFlow<Network state>, and check NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED and not only INTERNET. Having a network is not having internet: captive portals and dead Wi-Fi report connected. So I use connectivity as a hint for UI and retry timing, never as a gate for attempting a request.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: registerDefaultNetworkCallback needs API 24+. Callbacks: onAvailable, onLost, onCapabilitiesChanged. NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED means the system probed and reached the internet; NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET only means the network is configured for it. Also track metered (NOT_METERED) for big downloads. Needs ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE. Unregister in awaitClose; share with stateIn so there is one callback, not one per collector. The deprecated NetworkInfo.isConnected and CONNECTIVITY_ACTION broadcast should not be used.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun ConnectivityManager.onlineFlow(): Flow<Boolean> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
        override fun onCapabilitiesChanged(n: Network, c: NetworkCapabilities) {
            trySend(c.hasCapability(NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED))
        }
        override fun onLost(n: Network) { trySend(false) }
    }
    registerDefaultNetworkCallback(cb)
    awaitClose { unregisterNetworkCallback(cb) }
}.distinctUntilChanged()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blocking requests when "offline" (user may have working network the flag misjudges).
  • One callback per ViewModel (leaks and wasted work).
  • Emitting no initial value if already online at registration; verify behavior and seed with the current state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. VPN? → Check transports; VPN network can be the default with TRANSPORT_VPN.
  2. Where do you use it? → Offline banner, WorkManager constraints, retry backoff reset.
  3. Why not poll? → Battery and latency; callbacks are push.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes the flow. Senior explains validated vs available and refuses to gate requests on it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Users on captive hotel Wi-Fi saw "online" while every call timed out at 30 s.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app (2M DAU) ships shared-device support in a retail kiosk program. QA reports: log out of account A, log in as B, and the Orders tab briefly shows A's orders, then B's. Support also gets one privacy complaint. Code:

@Singleton
class OrdersRepository @Inject constructor(private val api: OrdersApi) {
    private var cache: List<Order> = emptyList()

    suspend fun orders(refresh: Boolean = false): List<Order> {
        if (refresh || cache.isEmpty()) cache = api.fetchOrders()
        return cache
    }
}

class LogoutUseCase @Inject constructor(private val session: SessionStore) {
    suspend operator fun invoke() { session.clearToken() }
}

Network log shows GET /orders for B only after the stale list rendered.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, fix it, and explain how you prevent the whole class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set cache to empty in logout." That fixes one repository; there are 15 others, plus Room, image cache and DataStore. It also ignores an in-flight fetchOrders() for A completing after logout and writing A's data into the cache.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which stores hold user data (memory, Room, DataStore, files, WebView cookies)? Is work running in app-scoped coroutines or WorkManager during logout? Any other process or widget reading data? Is multi-account a roadmap item (changes the fix shape)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: logout clears the token, the DB tables, and kills the process path to login via a fresh launch (Process.killProcess after cleanup is crude but effective for a kiosk hotfix).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) singleton in-memory cache survives logout (obvious); (b) in-flight request for A completes after logout and repopulates; (c) Room rows not cleared; (d) UI collects a flow with a stale stateIn replay; (e) HTTP cache returning A's /orders (red herring unless Cache-Control allows shared caching, check it).
  4. How I'd verify each: Repro with a debug breakpoint on cache assignment; LeakCanary-style heap dump after logout (Android Studio Profiler, filter Order) to see surviving instances; Network Inspector for ordering of A's late response; inspect databases/ via Device Explorer; check OkHttp Cache directory.
  5. Root cause: User-scoped data held in an app-scoped object with no owner tied to the session lifetime, and a logout that only revokes credentials. Plus a race: the coroutine from A's session has no cancellation on logout.
  6. Fix: Short term: a UserScoped cleanup contract; every holder registers and logout() awaits clear() on all. Long term: make user data live in a per-session container that is discarded (see Q279) so there is nothing to forget.
interface SessionScoped { suspend fun onSessionEnd() }

class LogoutUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val holders: Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards SessionScoped>, // @IntoSet bindings
    private val session: SessionStore,
    private val sessionScope: SessionCoroutineScope,
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke() {
        sessionScope.cancelAndJoin()                     // stop in-flight A work first
        holders.forEach { it.onSessionEnd() }
        session.clearToken()                              // credentials last, so cleanup calls still authorize if needed
    }
}
  1. Prevention: A unit test that injects every SessionScoped via Hilt multibinding and fails the build if a repository holding user data is not registered; a Konsist/lint rule that flags @Singleton classes with mutable collections not implementing the interface; an instrumented test "login A, logout, login B, assert no A data".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on killing the process as the design (it hides leaks and breaks ordering of writes). I would not clear in the ViewModels; they die with screens, the data does not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Logout fails halfway (disk full)? → Make cleanup idempotent, mark a "logout pending" flag in disk and resume at next launch before showing any user data.
  • Push notification for A arrives after logout? → Unregister the FCM token server-side first, and have the receiver check the session before rendering.
  • Remote logout (token revoked)? → Same pipeline, triggered by the auth layer's LoggedOut event.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A kiosk rollout leaked the previous shopper's last order total in a notification preview. The cache fix was trivial; the real finding was that nobody could list what held user data, so the team added a registry and a test that fails when a new holder is missing.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: clears one cache variable, never mentions in-flight work or other stores.
  • Hire: names all storage layers, cancels in-flight work, adds a cleanup contract.
  • Strong hire: also proposes a session-scoped container so cleanup is structural, adds an enforcing test, and handles failed/interrupted logout.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly must you tear down on logout in a production Android app, and in what order?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes completeness and ordering, the places seniors differ from mids.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stop work first, then clear data, then clear credentials, then change UI state. Work means coroutines and WorkManager jobs; data means memory caches, Room, DataStore, files, HTTP and image caches, WebView cookies; plus server-side unregistration (push token, device). Order matters so no in-flight work resurrects data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Checklist:

  1. Mark session Ending (so UI and interceptors stop issuing user requests).
  2. Cancel session-scoped coroutines (join them) and cancel user WorkManager work by tag.
  3. Server-side: revoke refresh token, delete FCM/device registration. Do this while the token is still valid; if offline, queue the revoke with the token captured, or accept server-side expiry.
  4. Clear in-memory holders (repositories, caches, StateFlows to initial state).
  5. Clear persistence: Room (clearAllTables() runs off main thread; or delete the per-user DB file), DataStore user prefs, files in user directories, Cache of OkHttp, Coil/Glide disk cache if URLs are user-specific, WebStorage/CookieManager, Keystore alias for user keys, notification channels/notifications showing user content, app shortcuts/widgets.
  6. Clear credentials last.
  7. Emit LoggedOut; routing resets the back stack. Keep what is device-level, not user-level: theme, locale, analytics consent (decide per product/legal).

Crash safety: write a "logout in progress" marker first and finish on next launch, so a crash between steps never leaves a half-cleaned logged-in-looking state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun logout() = withContext(NonCancellable) {   // cleanup must not be cancelled midway
    prefs.markLogoutPending()
    sessionScope.cancelAndJoin()
    workManager.cancelAllWorkByTag("user").result.await() // verify: ListenableFuture await via kotlinx-coroutines-guava
    runCatching { authApi.revoke() }                      // best effort
    holders.forEach { it.onSessionEnd() }
    db.clearAllTables()
    tokenStore.clear()
    prefs.clearLogoutPending()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• clearAllTables() on the main thread (Room throws).
  • Leaving WorkManager jobs that then upload as nobody/401-loop.
  • Forgetting external copies: notifications, share targets, widgets.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why NonCancellable? → If the calling screen's scope is cancelled mid-cleanup you get partial cleanup.
  2. Should theme reset? → No, device preference.
  3. Single DB vs per-user DB? → Per-user DB turns cleanup into a file delete and makes account switching easy (Q280).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "clear token and database". Senior: ordered, crash-safe, covers server and OS surfaces, with a enforcing test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Post-logout 401 loops from a surviving periodic upload worker drained battery and hammered the auth endpoint.

questions.promptHtml: How do you architect token attachment and refresh so concurrent requests don't break? (Keep it to the architecture; protocol details are A7.)

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know where auth logic belongs and what races exist.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Attach the access token in an OkHttp interceptor reading from a token provider; refresh in an Authenticator (called on 401) behind a single-flight lock, so N concurrent 401s trigger one refresh and the others reuse the result. If refresh definitively fails, the auth layer emits LoggedOut into the session state; nothing else decides that.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
request --> [AuthInterceptor: add Bearer from TokenStore]
                |
                v  401?
        [Authenticator.authenticate]
          lock {
            current = TokenStore.access
            if (current != tokenUsedByFailedRequest) -> retry with current (someone refreshed)
            else refresh() -> save -> retry
          }
          refresh fails (invalid_grant) -> SessionManager.logout()

Key points: compare the token the failed request used against the current one before refreshing (otherwise 10 parallel 401s cause 10 refreshes, and with rotating refresh tokens 9 will fail and may trip reuse detection). Authenticator is invoked by OkHttp and blocks a network thread, so it may use runBlocking bridging or a synchronized block; keep the refresh call on a client without the authenticator to avoid recursion. Distinguish failure types: network error (keep session, retry later) vs invalid_grant/401 on refresh (logout). Store tokens encrypted (Keystore-backed), not in plain prefs. Proactive refresh by expires_at reduces 401s but cannot replace the reactive path (clock skew, revocation).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class TokenAuthenticator @Inject constructor(
    private val tokens: TokenStore,
    private val refresher: TokenRefresher,   // uses a separate OkHttpClient
    private val sessions: SessionManager,
) : Authenticator {
    private val lock = Any()
    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? = synchronized(lock) {
        val used = response.request.header("Authorization")?.removePrefix("Bearer ")
        val current = tokens.accessToken()
        if (current != null && current != used) return response.retryWith(current)
        if (response.priorResponse != null) return null           // already retried once
        val fresh = refresher.refreshBlocking() ?: run { sessions.onRefreshRejected(); return null }
        response.retryWith(fresh.access)
    }
}
private fun Response.retryWith(t: String) = request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $t").build()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Refreshing inside the interceptor on every 401 without the compare.
  • Logging out on any IOException during refresh.
  • Infinite 401 loops (no priorResponse guard).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a separate client for refresh? → Same client would invoke the authenticator recursively.
  2. Where should the logout decision live? → One auth/session manager, not in screens.
  3. Multi-process (widgets, services)? → Lock is per process; use a cross-process store or one process owns refresh (verify design).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "interceptor adds header, authenticator refreshes". Senior: single-flight with token comparison, failure classification and session integration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: See the next scenario.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (800k DAU, backend uses rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection: replaying a used refresh token revokes the whole token family). After release 7.4, support sees users "randomly logged out", 1.9% of sessions per day versus 0.1% before. Pattern: mostly on app open after >1 h. Log excerpt (client, redacted):

12:01:03.114 POST /v2/auth/refresh -> 200
12:01:03.119 POST /v2/auth/refresh -> 200
12:01:03.402 POST /v2/auth/refresh -> 401 {"error":"invalid_grant","reason":"token_reuse"}
12:01:03.405 SessionManager: refresh rejected -> LoggedOut

Release 7.4 added a home screen that fires 6 parallel API calls on open. The Authenticator was written for the old home that made 1.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase token lifetime" (weakens security, hides the race) or "retry refresh on failure" (replays a used token, which reuse detection treats as theft).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is rotation + reuse detection server-enforced (yes per logs)? Does the Authenticator hold a lock? Which clients (phone app, widget, Wear) share a token store? Did refresh traffic change in 7.4 (count /refresh per session)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server side: relax reuse detection with a short grace window (e.g. accept the previous refresh token for ~10 s and return the same new pair) while the client fix ships. Client: remote-config the home screen to stagger calls (sequence the first call, then fan out) as a kill switch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no single-flight, parallel 401s each refresh; (b) the lock exists but the compare-token step is missing, so serialized callers each still refresh with the old token read before the lock; (c) a refresh response lost to a timeout and retried with the same old token; (d) two processes (app + widget worker) refreshing; (e) clock skew (red herring: logs show 200s then reuse).
  4. How I'd verify each: Count /refresh calls per session from analytics (expect 1, see 3 to 6 on affected sessions); correlate timestamps (three within 300 ms = parallel); read the Authenticator code and add a unit test with a MockWebServer returning 401 to six parallel calls and assert refresh count; check widget worker logs.
  5. Root cause: Reactive refresh without single-flight; with rotation, the first caller's refresh invalidates the token the others hold, the server sees reuse and kills the family.
  6. Fix: Short term: the synchronized compare-and-refresh from Q277. Long term: refresh owned by one coroutine-based component with a Mutex and an in-flight Deferred shared by all waiters; persist the new pair atomically before releasing waiters; treat network failure of refresh as retryable without discarding the old token; ask backend for idempotent refresh within a grace window.
class TokenRefresher(private val api: AuthApi, private val store: TokenStore) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    suspend fun refreshIfStillStale(usedToken: String?): String = mutex.withLock {
        val cur = store.access()
        if (cur != null && cur != usedToken) return cur   // someone else already refreshed
        val pair = api.refresh(store.refresh())
        store.save(pair)                                   // persist before unlocking
        pair.access
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Concurrency test with N parallel 401s; metric "refresh calls per session" with alert above 1.2; metric "forced logout rate" in release dashboard with staged rollout halt at 0.5%; code review rule: any new fan-out screen load tested against auth.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not longer token life. Not retrying a rejected refresh token. Not disabling reuse detection permanently, it is a real defense against token theft.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Refresh succeeded but the app was killed before saving? → Persist before using; with a server grace window the old token still works once.
  • Proactive refresh at 80% lifetime? → Helps; must go through the same single-flight.
  • Offline for 3 days, tokens expired? → Stay logged in locally, refresh on connectivity; logout only on explicit rejection.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "faster home" redesign tripled parallel calls and a rotation-based auth silently turned a latent race into a 20x logout spike; the fix was 15 lines, the lesson was a dashboard for refreshes per session.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes longer expiry or retry loops.
  • Hire: identifies parallel refresh race, adds lock and token comparison.
  • Strong hire: also coordinates a server grace window, instruments refresh-per-session, handles persistence-before-release and multi-process sources.

questions.promptHtml: How would you scope dependencies to a logged-in user session with Hilt or Dagger, and what are the alternatives?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes DI depth: lifetimes, component trees, and honesty about tooling limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hilt's built-in components do not include a user-session scope, so you either add a custom component (Hilt supports custom components with @DefineComponent, though it is more advanced; verify in current docs), use a manager in the Singleton component that builds a Dagger subcomponent or a plain container on login and drops it on logout, or avoid component-scoping and make user data classes take a UserId and live in a per-user DB. The point is that discarding the container discards all state, so nothing can be forgotten at logout.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Hilt hierarchy: SingletonComponent > ActivityRetainedComponent > ViewModelComponent/ActivityComponent > Fragment/View, plus ServiceComponent. You cannot insert a component in the middle, but you can define one with a Hilt component as parent and reach it via entry points.

Options:

Approach How Cost
Custom Hilt component @DefineComponent(parent = SingletonComponent::class) + builder, @UserScope, a UserComponentManager in Singleton creating on login Hilt docs describe it as advanced; entry points to fetch; modules @InstallIn(UserComponent::class)
Plain Dagger subcomponent / Anvil Manual component tree, more control Gives up Hilt conveniences for that subtree
Koin/kotlin-inject scopes Runtime scope or compile-time scoped component Different tooling
Manual "UserSession container" A class holding user repos built in a factory Simple, explicit, no DI magic
Parametrize by userId Singletons stay, data keyed by userId / per-user DB file Cleanest for storage, does not scope in-memory objects

Lifecycle: create on login or at startup when a session exists; ViewModels reach user-scoped deps through an injected UserComponentProvider (or a Flow<UserComponent?>); when the scope ends, cancel its CoroutineScope and drop the reference; GC reclaims the graph (verify no leaks with a heap dump).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Scope @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) annotation class UserScope

@UserScope
@DefineComponent(parent = SingletonComponent::class)
interface UserComponent {
    @DefineComponent.Builder interface Builder { fun session(@BindsInstance s: Session): Builder; fun build(): UserComponent }
}

@Singleton
class UserComponentManager @Inject constructor(private val builder: UserComponent.Builder) {
    @Volatile var component: UserComponent? = null; private set
    fun start(s: Session) { component = builder.session(s).build() }
    fun end() { component = null }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A @Singleton that depends on a @UserScope object (scope inversion: the longer-lived holds the shorter-lived, so it leaks and goes stale; Dagger rejects the direct form, but Provider/Lazy hacks bypass it).
  • Reading UserComponentManager.component!! after logout from a lingering coroutine.
  • Building the component on the main thread with heavy work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do ViewModels get user-scoped deps? → Via an entry point or a facade that exposes the current component; they must also end when the session ends.
  2. What cancels user coroutines? → A CoroutineScope provided in @UserScope and cancelled in end().
  3. Is the complexity worth it? → For one logged-in account and a few user-bound repos, a plain userId-keyed design is simpler; scope only when many objects share user lifetime.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "just use @Singleton and clear it". Senior shows how a scope makes the cleanup structural and can name the Hilt limits and alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that scoped by hand regularly found one forgotten singleton holding the last user's data; component discard removed that class of bug.

questions.contextHtml: A workplace chat app (1.2M DAU) adds multi-account (up to 5 accounts, instant switching like Slack). Today: one Room DB, one DataStore, singletons for repositories, one OkHttp client with a single token, FCM token registered per user. 6% of devices are 3 GB RAM or less. Requirement: switching under 300 ms perceived, notifications for all accounts continue arriving, no data bleed between accounts, offline data kept per account. PM also wants a "switch from a notification tap" flow.
questions.promptHtml: Design the account architecture and how you would migrate from the single-account design under live traffic.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear everything and log in again on switch" (fails the 300 ms and offline requirements) or "add an accountId column to every table" with no plan for the singletons and in-flight work.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do inactive accounts sync in the background, or only receive pushes? Are all five accounts "active" in memory? Can a notification tap target a non-active account? Any shared data across accounts (device settings, drafts)? Data-at-rest security requirement per account?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). First step is a spike measuring memory per account container to decide how many to keep warm.
  3. Hypotheses (design options), ranked: (a) per-account container (own DB file, own token, own OkHttp client, own scope) with one active at a time and others cold; (b) one DB with accountId on every table and singletons parametrized; (c) separate process per account (rejected: memory, complexity).
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype (a) and measure: switch latency (DB open + first query) with Macrobenchmark, heap per container in Profiler, and a test that logs in A and B and asserts zero cross reads.
  5. Root cause (of the current limitation): Identity is implicit global state: the singletons assume one user.
  6. Fix: Choose (a). An AccountManager in the app scope keeps activeAccountId (persisted) and a map accountId -> AccountContainer created lazily (DB file chat_<id>.db, token store key per account, client, CoroutineScope). Switching changes the active pointer, UI re-collects from activeAccount: StateFlow<AccountContainer> using flatMapLatest, and the previous container's foreground sync scope is cancelled but its DB is kept. Pushes: FCM payload carries accountId; a FirebaseMessagingService opens that container's DB only for the needed write and posts a notification with a PendingIntent that includes accountId; tap switches first, then navigates. Remove-account = cancel scope, delete DB file, wipe keys, unregister push for that account.
val activeContainer: StateFlow<AccountContainer?> =
    activeId.flatMapLatest { id -> flow { emit(id?.let(accountManager::containerFor)) } }
        .stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null)

fun ChatViewModel.messages() = activeContainer.filterNotNull()
    .flatMapLatest { it.messageRepo.observe(channelId) }

Migration under live traffic: step 1 introduce AccountContainer while there is still one account and hide behind a flag; step 2 move existing DB to the per-account file on first launch (copy then switch, keep the old as backup for one release); step 3 move tokens; step 4 re-register push per account; step 5 enable adding accounts for 1% then ramp. 7. Prevention: Konsist rule that code in feature modules may not inject DAO/api singletons directly, only the container facade; cross-account bleed test in CI; crash and ANR dashboards segmented by account count. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Per-container DB costs disk and open time but gives trivial wipe and isolation; accountId-column design is smaller but one missed WHERE leaks data, and cleanup becomes a slow delete. I would not keep all five containers hot on low-RAM devices; I'd evict LRU.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Switching latency at 800 ms? → Pre-open the most likely target DB, keep a skeleton UI from last cached state, move heavy init off the critical path.
  • Shared push token across accounts? → Register per account if backend supports it; otherwise route by accountId in payload.
  • Rollback of the migration? → Keep the old DB until two clean releases; flag allows return to single-account.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A multi-account launch missed that an ImageLoader cache was keyed by URL only, and signed avatar URLs in one workspace were served in another. Isolation had to include caches, not just DBs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: clear-and-relogin or global accountId hack, ignores notifications.
  • Hire: per-account container/DB, active pointer, push routing.
  • Strong hire: quantifies memory and latency, covers migration steps and rollback, and isolation of caches and background work.

questions.promptHtml: Features in different modules need to react to each other's changes (cart updated, user blocked, profile edited). Is a shared flow or event bus a good idea? What do you do instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests coupling awareness and whether you know the difference between events and state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A global event bus is hidden coupling: anyone can emit, anyone can listen, nobody can see the contract, delivery depends on who is subscribed at that moment, and nothing survives process death. I prefer shared state in a repository that owns the data: features observe a StateFlow/Flow from it and call methods to change it. If it truly is a command or notification, I use an explicit interface in a shared API module.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problems with an EventBus or app-wide MutableSharedFlow:

  • Delivery: with replay = 0 a screen that is in the background or not yet collecting misses the event forever. With replay > 0 it gets stale events replayed on re-collect.
  • Ownership: no single owner of the truth, so two features can disagree about "cart size".
  • Traceability: no call graph; "who triggers this refresh?" needs a grep over the whole app.
  • Testing and process death: events are not persisted, state is.

Better, in order:

  1. State in the owning repository: CartRepository.cart: StateFlow<Cart>. Profile screen edits call UserRepository.updateName(), every observer updates automatically. This is the "events are state" view of unidirectional data flow.
  2. Explicit contracts in an api module: interface CartNavigator, interface ProfileUpdates { fun onUpdated(): Flow<Unit> }, so dependencies are declared and DI-visible.
  3. Event stream only for real one-shot signals that cross features, with a documented owner and a single emitter, and a thought-through delivery policy.
// state in owner
@Singleton class CartRepository @Inject constructor(...) {
    private val _cart = MutableStateFlow(Cart.Empty)
    val cart: StateFlow<Cart> = _cart.asStateFlow()
    fun add(item: Item) = _cart.update { it + item }
}
// consumers in other modules depend on the interface in :cart:api
class BadgeViewModel @Inject constructor(cart: CartRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val count = cart.cart.map { it.size }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), 0)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the bus to avoid thinking about module dependencies, ending with every module depending on a core-events blob.
  • Using SharedFlow(replay = 1) as pseudo-state without conflation semantics.
  • Forgetting events emitted before the listener's screen is created.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Isn't a repository flow just a bus? → It carries current state with one owner and replay of the latest, not a stream of arbitrary commands.
  2. When is an event right? → Analytics, "force refresh now", or a push-triggered action, with one documented producer.
  3. Two features need each other's data (circular)? → Extract the shared model/interface into a lower api module; never let features depend on each other.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use a SharedFlow instead of EventBus library". Senior: replace the event with owned state and explicit contracts, and keep events for real one-shots.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Cart badge stayed stale for users who added items while the tab was not collected, a miss caused by replay = 0.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (500k DAU). The checkout module tells the home module to clear its "reorder" banner after payment using an app-wide flow. QA: pay for an order, go home, banner often still shows; sometimes after rotating it reappears; after backgrounding for 20 minutes the banner is gone then returns on relaunch.

@Singleton
class AppEvents @Inject constructor() {
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<AppEvent>(replay = 0)
    val events: SharedFlow<AppEvent> = _events
    suspend fun emit(e: AppEvent) = _events.emit(e)
}

// Checkout
class CheckoutViewModel(private val events: AppEvents) : ViewModel() {
    fun onPaid() = viewModelScope.launch { events.emit(AppEvent.OrderPlaced) }
}

// Home
class HomeViewModel(events: AppEvents) : ViewModel() {
    var showReorderBanner by mutableStateOf(true)
    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            events.events.collect { if (it is AppEvent.OrderPlaced) showReorderBanner = false }
        }
    }
}

Analytics show 11% of paying users see a stale banner.
questions.promptHtml: Why is this happening and how would you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set replay = 1." That replays OrderPlaced to every future collector (a new HomeViewModel after process death never needed it, and the first one would be dismissed forever or reapplied incorrectly) and still leaves banner state in a ViewModel that dies.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Home's ViewModel alive while Checkout is on top (nav back stack)? Does the banner depend on server data (reorder eligibility)? Should the banner come back after the next order delivered? Does the same event drive anything else?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make Home re-evaluate banner from the data on resume (the last order timestamp) so stale UI self-corrects; ship via a fast patch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Home's ViewModel is not collecting when emission happens (destroyed or not yet created; replay = 0 drops the event); (b) the banner flag is in-memory ViewModel state with default true, so rotation/process death reset it; (c) emit suspends until subscribers take it; no subscribers means it completes immediately and the event is lost; (d) analytics bug (red herring if banner data conflicts).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in emit and collector with timestamps; Layout Inspector plus a test that navigates Home -> Checkout -> Home using a nav test rule; write a unit test that emits before collecting and asserts the banner (it fails); kill the process with adb shell am kill and reopen.
  5. Root cause: A fact ("the user has an order placed since the banner was shown") was modeled as a transient event with no owner and no persistence, and then mirrored in a ViewModel field whose default does not reflect truth.
  6. Fix: Derive the banner from data, not from a signal.
class HomeViewModel(orders: OrderRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val showReorderBanner: StateFlow<Boolean> = orders.lastOrderAt
        .map { last -> last == null || last < Clock.System.now() - 7.days }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), false)
}

Checkout writes the order through OrderRepository (disk is truth), Home observes. No bus. 7. Prevention: A lint/Konsist rule banning new MutableSharedFlow in @Singleton classes without a review tag; a test pattern "emit-before-collect" for any remaining event; an architecture guideline "facts are state". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add replay = 1 or extraBufferCapacity hacks, nor a cleverer event library. A little persistence cost is cheaper than stale UI.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• It really is a one-shot "show a thank-you toast"? → Keep it local to checkout's result screen with the event consumed as state (flag + acknowledge), see the one-off event chunk.
  • Banner must disappear instantly in the same session before disk write? → The repository updates its in-memory StateFlow first and persists asynchronously.
  • Many consumers? → State in repository still works; no fan-out code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "refresh feed" event bus in a large app had 14 emitters and 9 collectors; nobody could explain a double-refresh bug until it was replaced with a lastModified state and consumers reacting to it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes replay or buffer parameters.
  • Hire: identifies lost event and non-durable flag, derives from repository state.
  • Strong hire: also explains emit semantics with no subscribers, process death behavior, adds prevention rules.

questions.promptHtml: How do you handle language/locale and other configuration state (theme, font scale) as app-wide state? What happens to the UI when it changes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of per-app language APIs and recreation behavior, plus where the preference lives.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The user's language choice is a persisted preference applied through the platform, not an in-memory field: AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales() (AppCompat 1.6+), which on API 33+ delegates to LocaleManager and on older versions is stored by AppCompat when autoStoreLocales is enabled via its service metadata. Applying it recreates activities, so screens must restore state. Theme is a DataStore preference exposed as app-scoped state and applied at the root.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Android 13 (API 33) added per-app language preferences in system settings and LocaleManager. AppCompat 1.6.0 backports AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat) and getApplicationLocales(). For devices below API 33 to persist the choice you declare the AppLocalesMetadataHolderService with autoStoreLocales = true in the manifest, or you store and re-apply it yourself at startup (verify exact manifest snippet in the official per-app language guide, I could not load it during research).
  • A locale change is a configuration change: the Activity is recreated (unless you declare configChanges, discouraged). Therefore anything in the UI must survive recreation: ViewModel state fine, remember state lost unless rememberSaveable.
  • Prefer not to hold your own Locale singleton copy; ask the platform (Configuration/LocalConfiguration in Compose). Date, number and currency formatting should read the current locale per call or from a recomposing source, not a cached formatter built at startup.
  • Theme: AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode() for the View system also recreates; in Compose, read the stored ThemeMode flow and pick darkColorScheme at the root (also see cold-start flash in the following scenarios).
  • Font scale and display size are system-driven; test at 200% font scale.
  • Server-side content language and push notification language need the choice synced; do not rely on Accept-Language alone from an old cache.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun setLanguage(tag: String) {
    AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags(tag)) // e.g. "hi-IN"
}
// Compose: reading locale-dependent formatting
@Composable fun Price(v: Double) {
    val locale = LocalConfiguration.current.locales[0]
    Text(NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale).format(v))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating a Context wrapper with a custom Locale in attachBaseContext (the pre-2022 hack; fragile with Compose and WebView).
  • Caching SimpleDateFormat/NumberFormat in a singleton so a locale change leaves stale formatting.
  • Forgetting RTL layout direction for Arabic/Hebrew.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does changing language kill the process? → No, it recreates activities; the process and singletons stay.
  2. Why does my dialog text stay in the old language? → The string was resolved with an old Context/cached before the change.
  3. Language for notifications? → Resolve at post time with the current app locale, or send localized payload from the server.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes a Locale wrapper. Senior uses the platform API, knows it recreates, and treats formatting caches and server sync as part of the same state.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cached NumberFormat produced Indian-rupee grouping for users who switched to English-US inside the app.

questions.subtopic: Process death restoration of app-wide state
questions.promptHtml: Design how app-wide state is restored after process death so any screen in the restored back stack works without the user re-logging in.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The hardest realistic lifecycle problem in this chunk; separates theory from experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The restored Activity can start before anything has re-hydrated, so I make initialization explicit and idempotent: durable truth on disk (tokens, user, preferences), a single bootstrap that loads it into app-scoped holders exposed as Unknown -> Ready state, and screens that restore from IDs in saved state and tolerate Unknown by showing loading, not crashing. No screen may assume a login-time in-memory object exists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sequence after the OS kills the process and the user returns:

 new process: Application.onCreate (DI graph built, light work only)
   -> restored Activity.onCreate (savedInstanceState + back stack from nav/SavedStateHandle)
   -> ViewModels recreated (SavedStateHandle has IDs)
   -> screen asks repositories for data
 meanwhile: bootstrap coroutine reads DataStore/Room -> session = Ready

Design rules:

  1. Disk is truth for user, tokens, preferences, flags; memory is a cache of it.
  2. One bootstrap (App Startup Initializer or a lazily started app-scoped coroutine) with a Bootstrap.state: StateFlow<Unknown|Ready|Failed>. Keep Application.onCreate cheap; do not block on disk.
  3. Screens gate on state, not on timing: a restored deep screen shows a loading placeholder until Ready; routing decisions (still logged in?) re-evaluate.
  4. Saved state carries IDs only (order id, query), as the official guide advises (small, primitive, written when the Activity stops); everything else is reloaded.
  5. Idempotent init: running bootstrap twice or after a partial run must be safe.
  6. Remote config and feature flags: use last cached values from disk at start, refresh in background; do not re-gate a restored screen on a fresh network fetch.
  7. Test: adb shell am kill <package> with the app backgrounded on a deep screen, then reopen; also "Don't keep activities" for the activity part.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class OrderDetailViewModel @Inject constructor(
    handle: SavedStateHandle, boot: Bootstrap, repo: OrderRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val id: String = checkNotNull(handle["orderId"])
    val ui: StateFlow<OrderUi> = boot.state
        .flatMapLatest { s -> if (s is Ready) repo.observe(id).map(OrderUi::Content) else flowOf(OrderUi.Loading) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), OrderUi.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Initializing session in the login flow only, so the restored deep screen has no session.
  • Heavy synchronous init in Application.onCreate inflating cold start and ANR risk.
  • Putting whole objects in SavedStateHandle (transaction size, jank).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if bootstrap fails (corrupt DB)? → Failed state with recovery path: wipe local cache and re-login, never crash loop.
  2. Where do WorkManager jobs fit? → They survive death by design; they must not assume in-memory singletons (they get DI-created ones).
  3. Multi-activity apps? → Same bootstrap shared; each entry point observes it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use SavedStateHandle". Senior: designs the hydration order, gates on Ready, keeps saved state minimal, tests with real process kill.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash clusters "after long background" disappeared once the bootstrap state replaced implicit assumptions.

questions.subtopic: Process death restoration of app-wide state
questions.contextHtml:
Release 5.2 of a ride-hailing app (3M DAU). Crashlytics shows a new top crash: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property user has not been initialized at TripSummaryViewModel.<init>, 0.8% of sessions, 92% on Android 12-14, almost all with "app in background > 30 min" and a notification deep link into the Trip Summary screen. QA cannot reproduce by rotating or relaunching. Code:

object UserHolder { lateinit var user: User }   // set in LoginViewModel on success and in SplashActivity from cached profile

class TripSummaryViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val name = UserHolder.user.name
}

Release 5.2 moved the splash/profile hydration to run only when the launcher intent is MAIN, to speed up cold start by 120 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why only these sessions fail, how you stop the crash now, and how you fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a null check" (hides it, the screen shows blank name) or "make it by lazy" with no source of truth. Also blaming the notification library.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What intent starts the restored process (notification tap vs launcher)? Is the crash also in cold launch with deep link from a closed app? Rollout percentage and version split? Does 5.1 show the crash (it should not)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt rollout; server-side kill switch or hotfix that restores hydration for all entry points; rollback is acceptable since 5.1 was healthy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) process was killed, deep-link launch via notification bypasses SplashActivity hydration (matches the 5.2 change); (b) background thread race on lateinit; (c) obfuscation or R8 issue (red herring, crash is in app code with readable names); (d) OEM-specific kill behavior (red herring, spread across OEMs).
  4. How I'd verify each: Group crashes by launch intent/entry point custom key; reproduce with adb shell am kill com.app then adb shell am start -a VIEW -d "app://trip/123"; diff 5.1 vs 5.2 startup path; check the 120 ms startup change in the PR.
  5. Root cause: UserHolder is in-memory state treated as durable. The old design happened to hydrate on every launch through SplashActivity; the optimization made it conditional, exposing the fact that deep links start a new process without visiting the splash.
  6. Fix: Short term: hydrate in the Bootstrap that all entry points await (Q284). Long term: remove UserHolder; UserRepository.user: StateFlow<User?> from disk; the ViewModel takes the tripId from nav args and observes user as nullable state.
class TripSummaryViewModel @Inject constructor(
    handle: SavedStateHandle, users: UserRepository, trips: TripRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val tripId: String = checkNotNull(handle["tripId"])
    val ui = combine(users.user, trips.observe(tripId)) { u, t -> TripUi(u?.name.orEmpty(), t) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), TripUi.Loading)
}
  1. Prevention: A CI instrumented test that kills the process and deep-links to each registered route; lint ban on lateinit in objects; a "startup path" checklist in PR template (any init moved off the splash needs all entry points reviewed); crash alert by version with staged rollout gates (halt at 0.2% new crash cluster).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not keeping the 120 ms gain by skipping hydration; I would get it back by making hydration async and the UI tolerant of Loading. I would not add try/catch around the access.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same crash from a widget or a WorkManager job? → They are entry points too; they must call the same bootstrap or use disk-backed repositories.
  • Hydration reads encrypted prefs slowly (80 ms)? → Cache non-sensitive profile fields in plain DataStore, keep tokens in Keystore-backed storage, load async.
  • How do you know the fix works in production? → Crash cluster rate by version and an event "bootstrap_wait_ms" p95.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A startup optimization that skipped a seemingly redundant init shipped cleanly through QA because every test launched from the launcher icon; the real traffic had 40% of sessions entering through notifications.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds null check or blames device.
  • Hire: ties crash to process death plus entry-point bypass, restores hydration.
  • Strong hire: removes the holder for disk-backed state, adds kill-and-deeplink CI test, segments by entry point, preserves startup gain.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (4M DAU, 35% of users on dark mode setting "Dark" chosen in-app). Users complain of a white flash at launch before the dark theme appears. Perf dashboard: time to first frame p50 = 520 ms; theme DataStore read p95 = 180 ms on mid-tier devices (3-4 GB RAM). Code:

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            val mode by themeRepo.theme.collectAsState(initial = ThemeMode.System)
            AppTheme(darkTheme = mode.isDark(isSystemInDarkTheme())) { AppRoot() }
        }
    }
}

Product wants the flash gone without adding more than 30 ms to cold start. Splash is the Android 12+ SplashScreen API via installSplashScreen().
questions.promptHtml: Why does it flash, and what are your options and trade-offs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Read it with runBlocking in onCreate" with no thought for cost, or "make the window background black" which breaks light-mode users.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the system default for these users (many "Dark" selectors also run system dark)? Is the flash on every launch or only cold? Can the theme be known earlier (a cached copy)? Is 30 ms a hard budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Use setKeepOnScreenCondition { themeRepo.theme.value == null } so the splash covers the 100-180 ms read instead of showing the wrong theme; that moves the wait to the splash, which users read as startup, not a glitch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) initial value System renders light first, then dark arrives (matches); (b) window background from the theme XML is light before Compose draws (also contributes); (c) DataStore first read slow due to cold file/IO (affects duration, not cause); (d) recomposition cost (red herring, one recomposition).
  4. How I'd verify each: Screen recording at 60 fps frame-stepped; Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric before/after; Perfetto trace for the DataStore read thread; temporarily hardcode initial dark and see the flash vanish for dark users but appear for light users (confirms (a)).
  5. Root cause: Honest initial state was missing: the code claims System while the true value is unknown, so the first frame is drawn with a wrong guess.
  6. Fix: Options compared: | Option | Cost | Result | |---|---|---| | Keep splash until value loaded (nullable state) | +100-180 ms perceived, only first read | Correct first frame | | Mirror theme in a tiny SharedPreferences read synchronously in Application/onCreate | ~1-5 ms typical for a small file (measure) | Correct first frame, keeps DataStore as truth | | runBlocking { first() } on main | Blocks, up to 180 ms, ANR risk on slow disks | Works, risky | | Window background from night-qualified resources | 0 cost | Fixes the system-dark case, not in-app override | I would pick: keep DataStore as truth, write the mode also to a small synchronous mirror (or use AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode early which persists its own value for the View system), and gate the splash on a null state as a fallback. Night-qualified window background covers the remaining flash.
val splash = installSplashScreen()
val initial = themeMirror.read() // sync, tiny
splash.setKeepOnScreenCondition { themeRepo.theme.value == null && initial == null }
setContent {
    val mode by themeRepo.theme.collectAsState()
    AppTheme(darkTheme = (mode ?: initial ?: ThemeMode.System).isDark(isSystemInDarkTheme())) { AppRoot() }
}
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark startup test in CI with a budget (p50 and p95 gate); rule that any "default value" for persisted state must be nullable/unknown; a screenshot test of first frame for dark preference.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The mirror duplicates truth (risk of divergence); I would write both in one repository method and read DataStore as authority after load. I would not block with runBlocking on every start.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User changes theme in settings? → Write both stores, app state updates via the flow, Activity does not need recreation in Compose.
  • 30 ms budget exceeded by the mirror? → Measure first; if so, move the read into a ContentProvider-free Initializer that runs in parallel with other startup work.
  • Locale has the same issue? → Yes, same pattern; platform stores it, see the locale question.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A white flash complaint ranked below crashes for months until a rating-trend analysis tied it to 1-star reviews from dark-mode users; the fix was a 3-line sync mirror and a startup benchmark.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: hardcodes a background color or blocks the main thread blindly.
  • Hire: identifies wrong initial state, uses splash gating or a sync mirror.
  • Strong hire: compares options with measured costs, keeps DataStore as truth, adds startup benchmark gate.
